question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what observable property do the authors use to identify the finest star anise oils?
reference_answer: They consider star anise oils with a higher solidifying point to be the best.
supporting_passage:
Since anethol is the
most valuable constituent, and the solidifying point of the oil is
roughly proportional to its anethol content, oils with a higher
solidifying point are the best.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, how do the authors arrange and burn a sample of bitter-almond oil when testing it for chlorine?
reference_answer: They saturate a loosely rolled coil of filter paper with the oil, burn it in a small porcelain dish, and cover the dish with an inverted beaker moistened inside with distilled water.
required_key_points: A loosely rolled coil of filter paper saturated with the oil
Burn it in a small porcelain dish
An inverted beaker moistened inside with distilled water covers the dish
supporting_passage:
To test for chlorine in
a sample, a small coil of filter paper, loosely rolled, is saturated
with the oil, and burnt in a small porcelain dish, covered with an
inverted beaker, the inside of which is moistened with distilled water.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what aldehyde-content ranges do the authors assign to each of the three grades of cassia oil sold commercially?
reference_answer: The best grade has 80-85 per cent. aldehydes, the second 75-80 per cent., and the lowest 70-75 per cent.
supporting_passage:
Three grades are
usually offered, the best containing 80-85 per cent. aldehydes, the
second quality, 75-80 per cent., and the lowest grade, 70-75 per cent.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what method do the authors specify for measuring the cineol in eucalyptus globulus oil?
reference_answer: The cineol is combined with phosphoric acid, pressed, decomposed with hot water, and then measured in its liberated form.
required_key_points: Pressing, then decomposition with hot water
supporting_passage:
Specific gravity at 15 deg. C., 0.910-0.930; optical
rotation, +1 deg. to +10 deg.; soluble in 2 to 3 parts of 70 per cent. alcohol;
cineol (estimated by combination with phosphoric acid, pressing,
decomposing with hot water, and measuring the liberated cineol), not
less than 50 per cent.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what trade name was used for the exceptionally fine geranium oil that the authors favour for high-class soaps?
reference_answer: It was sold under the name "Geranium-sur-Rose."
supporting_passage:
A specially fine article is sold by a few
essential oil firms under the name of "Geranium-sur-Rose," which as its
name implies, is supposed to be geranium oil distilled over roses. This
is particularly suitable for use in high-class soaps.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what ester-content observation do the authors cite to challenge the older way of judging lavender oil quality?
reference_answer: They observe that some of the finest lavender oils contain less than 30 per cent. of esters.
required_key_points: Some of the finest oils contain less than 30 per cent. of esters
supporting_passage:
There was at one time a theory that the higher the proportion of ester
the better the oil, but this theory has now to a very large extent
become discredited, and there is no doubt that some of the finest oils
contain less than 30 per cent. of esters.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, which substances do the authors describe as making up most of patchouli oil while having little effect on its distinctive odour?
reference_answer: The two substances are patchouliol and cadinene.
supporting_passage:
The
oil consists to the extent of 97 per cent. of patchouliol and cadinene,
which have little influence on its odour, and the bodies responsible for
its persistent and characteristic odour have not yet been isolated.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what effects on rosemary oil do the authors associate with distilling stalks along with the leaves?
reference_answer: Doing so reduces specific gravity and borneol content, while increasing the proportion of the laevo-rotatory constituent laevo-pinene.
supporting_passage:
The properties of the oils vary with their source, and also with the
parts of the plant distilled, distillation of the stalks as well as the
leaves tending to reduce the specific gravity and borneol content, and
increase the proportion of the laevo-rotatory constituent (laevo-pinene).

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what specific-gravity threshold do the authors use to identify loss of safrol from sassafras oil?
reference_answer: A specific gravity below 1.06 indicates that safrol has been removed.
supporting_passage:
The removal of safrol, either intentionally or by
accident, owing to cooling of the oil and consequent deposition of the
safrol, is readily detected by the reduction of the specific gravity
below 1.06.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what minimum ester content do the authors stipulate for amyl salicylate used in perfumery?
reference_answer: They stipulate not less than 97 per cent. ester, calculated as amyl salicylate.
required_key_points: Not less than 97 per cent. ester
supporting_passage:
It has the specific gravity at
15 deg. C., 1.052-1.054; optical rotation, +1 deg. 16' to +1 deg. 40'; refractive
index at 20 deg. C., 1.5056; and should contain not less than 97 per cent.
ester, calculated as amyl salicylate.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, why do the authors suggest that artificial jasmine oil might be better than oil prepared from actual flowers?
reference_answer: They suggest that the natural flower odour is so delicate that it may suffer slight decomposition during the preparation process.
required_key_points: The extremely delicate natural odour undergoes slight decomposition during preparation from the flowers
supporting_passage:
_Jasmine._--This is one of the few cases in which the artificial oil is
probably superior to that obtained from the natural flowers, possibly
due to the extreme delicacy of the odour, and its consequent slight
decomposition during preparation from the flowers.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, why do the authors object to adding wax solely to make artificial rose oil resemble the natural product?
reference_answer: The wax is inodorous and therefore brings no benefit, while in cold weather it also makes it necessary to melt the oil before use.
required_key_points: The wax is inodorous and provides no advantage
The oil must first be melted in cold weather
supporting_passage:
In some cases stearopten or
other wax is added, to render the oil more similar in appearance to the
natural article, but as these are inodorous, no advantage is gained in
this way, and there is, further, the inconvenience in cold weather of
having to first melt the oil before use.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, which two trace substances do the authors say accompany vanillin in the vanilla bean?
reference_answer: They identify benzoic acid and heliotropin.
supporting_passage:
It has a strong characteristic
odour, and occurs, associated with traces of benzoic acid and
heliotropin, in the vanilla bean.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, which two essential oils do the authors attribute to Holland in their list of European perfume-oil sources?
reference_answer: They name caraway and clove oils.
supporting_passage:
Thus,
from Africa we have geranium and clove oils; from America, bay, bois de
rose, Canadian snake root, cedarwood, linaloe, peppermint, petitgrain,
and sassafras; from Asia, camphor, cassia, cinnamon, patchouli,
sandalwood, star anise, ylang-ylang, and the grass oils, _viz._,
citronella, lemongrass, palmarosa, and vetivert; from Australia,
eucalyptus; while in Europe there are the citrus oils, bergamot, lemon,
and orange, produced by Sicily, aspic, lavender, neroli, petitgrain, and
rosemary by France, caraway and clove by Holland, anise by Russia, and
otto of rose by Bulgaria.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, above what phenol content do the authors consider clove oil less satisfactory in odour, and what cause do they give?
reference_answer: Oils with more than 93 per cent. phenols are less satisfactory because this high proportion is obtained at the expense of decomposition of some sesquiterpene.
required_key_points: Decomposition of some of the sesquiterpene
supporting_passage:
While within certain limits the value of
this oil is determined by its eugenol content, oils containing more than
93 per cent. phenols are usually less satisfactory in odour, the high
proportion of phenols being obtained at the expense of the decomposition
of some of the sesquiterpene.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what characteristic makes East Indian lemon-grass oil preferable to the West Indian product in the authors' judgement?
reference_answer: They prefer East Indian oil because it is more soluble in alcohol.
supporting_passage:
_Lemon-grass_ (so-called _verbena_) oil, distilled from the grass
Andropogon citratus, which is grown in India and, more recently, in the
West Indies. The oils from these two sources differ somewhat in their
properties, and also in value, the former being preferred on account of
its greater solubility in alcohol.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what alcohol-solubility characteristics do the authors report for West Australian sandalwood oil?
reference_answer: It is insoluble in 70 per cent. alcohol but readily dissolves in 1-2 volumes of 80 per cent. alcohol.
required_key_points: Readily dissolves in 1-2 volumes of 80 per cent. alcohol
supporting_passage:
West Australian.--Specific gravity at 15 deg. C., 0.950-0.968; optical
rotation, +5 deg. to +7 deg.; alcohols, calculated as santalol, 73-75 per cent.;
insoluble in 70 per cent. alcohol, but readily dissolves in 1-2 volumes
of 80 per cent. alcohol.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, which chemical was covered by the original artificial-musk patent of Baur cited by the authors?
reference_answer: It covered the tri-nitro-derivative of tertiary butyl xylene.
required_key_points: The tri-nitro-derivative of tertiary butyl xylene
supporting_passage:
The original patent of Baur, obtained in 1889, covered the
tri-nitro-derivative of tertiary butyl xylene.
